body.description: The village uses the communal inscription room to maintain a shared grain ledger. Residents record authorized withdrawals and completed collections during their single daily visit so that later visitors can determine what remains owed. One afternoon, part of the granary roof collapses and exposes several bins to rain. A resident inspecting the damage tells the grain keeper that grain from those bins must be distributed immediately. The keeper has already used the day's room visit and cannot alter the durable ledger until tomorrow. Emergency distribution therefore begins through interpersonal instructions. Initially this works: a resident told to collect a particular quantity can act while that exchange remains privately recallable. But the emergency itself increases conversation. People ask about damaged bins, available containers, household needs, and who has already collected grain. Each interpersonal exchange advances the recall limit for earlier exchanges. Some participants consequently lose the details of their authorization before acting, while others successfully collect grain but later lose the conversational context explaining why their withdrawal differed from the inscription. Residents who still have unused room visits can potentially preserve pieces of the emergency state, but only if they learn those pieces while they remain recallable and reach the room before consuming their own visit. The result is not necessarily total informational collapse; instead, the durable ledger becomes unevenly synchronized with reality. Some emergency withdrawals are recorded by informed residents, some remain absent, and some inscriptions may preserve outcomes without preserving enough context to determine how they relate to the original allocation. As further exchanges occur, missing links can become permanently unrecoverable. The next day, the village may know the physical quantity of grain remaining and possess a persistent ledger containing both old allocations and some emergency updates, yet still be unable to establish a unique history connecting them. Two households can plausibly claim that they were promised the same remaining allocation, with neither claim resolvable from surviving inscriptions and neither claimant able to recall the expired exchange that would settle the matter. The shared arrangement has therefore failed in a deeper way than simple record staleness: its history has become partially non-reconstructible. Restoring operation requires a new authoritative decision about present entitlements rather than discovering with certainty what the previous arrangement required. The village can continue using the inscription room, but the repaired allocation must begin from acknowledged uncertainty, because durable writing made after conversational information disappears cannot recreate details that were never inscribed.
